client: I've been having a really hard time since my breakup with Maria about three months ago, and honestly I'm not even sure where to start. The things I used to love, like going hiking with my friends on weekends, just don't feel the same anymore — I'll be out on a trail and it's like I'm just going through the motions, completely numb. I guess I agreed to try therapy, but part of me wonders if talking about it is actually going to change how I feel.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for being honest about your doubts — that actually takes a lot of courage, and it tells me you're already doing something meaningful by showing up. The way you describe hiking, going through the motions and feeling numb, really captures how grief after a breakup can quietly hollow out the things that once brought us joy. It makes complete sense that you'd wonder if talking can change that, and that's actually something we can explore together — because often the first step is just understanding what's happening in your mind, not forcing yourself to feel differently right away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, what you're saying about not forcing myself to feel differently. But honestly, I'm not even sure what's happening in my mind half the time — it's like there's this fog and I can't really get a clear read on anything. And I keep going back and forth between thinking I should be over this by now and then feeling guilty for not being over it.
therapist: That fog you're describing is so real, and I can hear in the way you're speaking — there's a kind of racing, almost breathless quality to it — like your mind is working hard to make sense of something that just won't sit still. What you're caught in is actually a really common but painful trap: the idea that there's a timeline for grief, and that you're somehow failing by not meeting it. In CBT we'd gently challenge that thought — where did that rule come from, that you *should* be over this by now, and what's the evidence that it's actually true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... the rule came from other people, mostly. My coworkers kept saying things like "it's been six months, you must be feeling better by now," and I just started believing them, like their timeline was the right one. But when you ask me for evidence that it's actually true, I honestly don't have any — I just absorbed it and turned it into this pressure I carry around every single day.
therapist: That's a really significant realization — you just caught yourself absorbing someone else's expectation and carrying it as if it were a fact about you, and that takes genuine self-awareness to see. Your voice carries something that sounds like a quiet tension, almost like the weight of that pressure is sitting right there as you speak. Now that you can see this "rule" actually came from outside you and has no real evidence behind it, we can start to loosen its grip — because you get to define what your own healing looks like, not your coworkers.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's not that simple, you know? Like, even if I logically know the expectation came from them, I still have to face those people every day at work, and the pressure doesn't just disappear because I've named where it came from. It's almost like knowing the source makes me feel a little more lonely, actually, because now I realize I've been carrying something that was never even mine to carry.
therapist: What you just said about feeling more lonely after the realization — that's actually a profound and painful moment, and I can hear it in how softly you're speaking, like you're sitting with something heavy and tender all at once. You're absolutely right that insight doesn't make the daily reality disappear, and it's not supposed to — but what it *does* do is give you back something that was taken from you, which is the ability to choose how you relate to that pressure. And that loneliness you're feeling right now, that grief of realizing you've been carrying a burden that was never yours — that deserves to be honored, not rushed past.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure I fully understand what you mean by "choosing how I relate to the pressure." Like, the pressure is still there every day when I wake up and check my phone, hoping someone has reached out, and they haven't. I don't know how a choice changes that feeling of just... waiting and being disappointed over and over again.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with a kind of high, tight energy — tells me this particular pain, the waiting and the silence from your phone, is something that hits you fresh every single morning, and that's exhausting in a way that's hard to put into words. You're right to push back on what I said, because "choosing how you relate" can sound abstract when you're in the middle of something that concrete and recurring. What I mean is that right now your mind is interpreting that silence as confirmation of something — maybe that you're not worth reaching out to — and gently questioning *that* interpretation, not the feeling itself, is where the choice actually lives.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, that's... that's actually kind of close to what's happening. Like there's this voice that kicks in around 7am that says "see, nobody thought of you overnight, nobody woke up wanting to talk to you." And I know logically that people are just busy, but in that moment it doesn't feel like logic has any power over it at all.
therapist: That 7am voice is so specific and so cruel, and the way you're describing it — softly, carefully, like you're almost tiptoeing around it — tells me it carries a lot of weight even just in the naming of it. You've actually just identified something really important in CBT terms: that's an automatic thought, and the fact that logic feels powerless against it makes complete sense, because it's firing before you're even fully awake, before your rational mind has a chance to show up. The work isn't about silencing that voice with logic in the moment — it's about slowly, over time, building enough evidence against it that it starts to lose its authority.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about building evidence against it, but honestly... I'm not sure what evidence would even look like. Like, the voice doesn't really make a specific claim I can argue with — it's more like a feeling that just settles over everything, this heavy sense that I wasted another day, that I'm falling behind some invisible standard I can't even name. How do you build a case against something that vague?
therapist: That high, almost strained quality in your voice as you describe this feels like someone straining to see something just out of reach — and what you're naming is actually one of the hardest things to work with, because you're not fighting a thought, you're fighting an atmosphere. But here's something worth sitting with: that "invisible standard" you mentioned — even if you can't name it fully, *you* created the phrase "falling behind," which means somewhere there's an assumption that life is a race with a pace you're supposed to be keeping. What if we got curious together about where that standard came from, not to argue with the feeling, but just to shine a little light on the shape of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to go along with it, but honestly it also feels a little too neat, like if I just trace it back to where the standard came from, the feeling will somehow loosen its grip. I know intellectually that's probably not how it works, but the atmosphere you described is exactly right — it's not one specific thought I can argue with, it's more like the air I breathe. And I guess I'm a little skeptical that shining a light on where it came from will actually change anything, because I've thought about this before and it just feels like the standard is... everywhere, not from one place.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and I want to honor it rather than talk you out of it — because you're right, tracing something back to its origin isn't a cure, and I don't want to offer you something that feels tidy when your experience is genuinely not. What strikes me is that even as you're pushing back, there's something almost urgent in how you're speaking, like a part of you is working very hard to make sure I understand just how pervasive this feeling is — and I think that urgency matters, because it tells me this isn't something you want fixed with a neat framework, you want to feel genuinely less alone inside it. So maybe the question isn't how do we dismantle the standard, but rather — what would it feel like to move through a day without having to measure yourself against it at all, even just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, you're right that there's something urgent about it, and I don't totally know what to do with that. But when you ask what it would feel like to move through a day without measuring myself, I honestly can't even picture it — like, the measuring is so automatic that I'm not sure there's a "me" separate from it. It's almost like asking what water would feel like without being wet.
therapist: The image you just used — water without being wet — is remarkable, and the way you said it, softly but quickly, like it came from somewhere deep and certain, tells me this isn't just a metaphor to you, it's the closest you've gotten to the truth of what this feels like. What you're describing touches on something really fundamental in CBT, which is that sometimes the most ingrained beliefs aren't thoughts we *have*, they're identities we *are* — and that's both why they're so hard to shift and also why noticing them, the way you just did, is genuinely significant work. You may not be able to picture a "you" separate from the measuring yet, but the fact that you can observe it, name it, even find a metaphor for it, means there *is* a part of you standing slightly outside it — and that's the part we're talking to right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to hold onto that — the idea that there's some version of me that exists outside all the measuring and comparing. But it feels so small, that part, like it's just a tiny observer watching from a corner while the rest of me runs the numbers constantly. And honestly, I'm not sure that little observer has any real power to change anything, it just... watches.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of high, almost fragile quality — alongside the stillness of what you're describing, feels like someone who is both urgent and exhausted at the same time, like that little observer is working very hard just to stay visible. But I want to gently offer this: the observer doesn't need to be powerful to be important — in fact, the fact that it *watches* means it hasn't been consumed, and in CBT we'd say that witnessing yourself is not a small thing, it's actually the very beginning of change. That part of you found the water metaphor, that part of you pushed back on my neat frameworks, that part of you is here right now — it may feel like it's watching from a corner, but it's been quietly doing a lot of work today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
